column2: There the bright Apsarases, untiring through all time, with spotless faces, sport in stainless pastimes.
Month by month, lord of men, gods and Gandharvas come to that holy tirtha frequented by Brahmanas.
There Gandharvas and hosts of Apsarases were seen, O king, gathered together as they came, at their ease.
There gods and ancestors rejoice, repeatedly showered with holy, divine flowers.
That auspicious playground of those Apsarases, O king, on the best bank of the Sarasvati, is famed as Subhumika.
Bathing there and giving wealth to Brahmanas, Madhava heard the divine song and the sound of instruments.
There Gandharvas led by Vishvavasu, rich in austerity, make dance, music and song of great charm.
There the plough-bearer gave to Brahmanas wealth of many kinds—goats, sheep, cows, mules, camels, gold and silver.
Having fed the twice-born to their desire and satisfied them with great wealth, Madhava set out with the Brahmanas, praised by them.
From that Gandharva tirtha the mighty-armed subduer of foes, wearing a single earring, came to the great tirtha Gargasrota.
There the aged Garga, his soul refined by austerity, acquired knowledge of time, the courses of the luminaries and their deviations,
and of dreadful and auspicious omens, Janamejaya; at that auspicious tirtha of the Sarasvati the great soul laid them down, and from his name that tirtha is remembered as Gargasrota.
There the sages of good vows, O king, ever attended the greatly fortunate Garga for the knowledge of time.
Going there, great king, Bala, anointed with white, gave wealth duly to the sages of purified souls,
and having given Brahmanas various foods, the blue-clad, greatly renowned one went to Shankhatirtha.
There the strong, palm-bannered one saw the great Shankha, a tree risen like great Meru, resembling a white mountain, frequented by hosts of sages, grown on the bank of the Sarasvati.
There Yakshas, Vidyadharas, Rakshasas of immense might, and Pishachas of immense strength—thousands of perfected ones—
all give up food and at due times eat the fruit of that tree, by vows and restraints.
Having attained those various restraints, roaming each by himself, unseen by men, they moved about, bull among men.
Thus, lord of men, that tree is famed in this world, and there is the Sarasvati's purifying tirtha, renowned in the world.
At that tirtha the tiger of the Yadus gave to the renowned ones copper and iron vessels and clothes of various kinds,
and having honoured the twice-born and being honoured by the ascetics, the plough-bearer came, O king, to the holy Dvaitavana.
Going there and seeing the sages in diverse garb, Bala bathed in the water and honoured the Brahmanas.
Likewise giving the Brahmanas very abundant provisions, Bala then proceeded, O king, to the south of the Sarasvati.
Having gone not far, the mighty-armed, greatly renowned, righteous-souled Achyuta came to the tirtha Nagadhanva.
There is the abode of Vasuki, king of serpents, of great splendour, O great king, filled with many serpents; there were fourteen thousand perfected sages.
There the gods assembled and consecrated Vasuki, best of serpents and king of all serpents, duly; there, Kaurava, there is no fear of serpents.
There too, having duly given Brahmanas heaps of jewels, he went to the eastern region, O king, blazing with his own splendour.
Bathing many times, glad, at those tirthas, the plough-bearer gave wealth to the twice-born and went on to the great ascetics.
Having saluted the hosts of sages there, the plough-bearer, Rama, then went to a great tirtha frequented by sages,
where the Sarasvati once turned back, facing the other way, to meet the great-souled sages of Naimisha.
Seeing that best of rivers turned back there, the plough-bearer, Bala anointed in white, became astonished, O king.
[Janamejaya said:] "Why did the Sarasvati turn back, Brahmana, facing the other way? I wish to hear all this explained, best of Adhvaryus.
And for what reason was the delight of the Yadus astonished there? How did this best of rivers turn back, best of the twice-born?"
[Vaishampayana said:] "In the Krita age of old, O king, the ascetics of Naimisha were engaged in a long sacrificial session of twelve years, and many sages, O king, gathered there.
Having dwelt in that session duly, when the twelve-year session at Naimisha ended, many sages came there for the sake of the tirthas.
Because of the great number of sages, lord of men, the tirthas on the southern bank of the Sarasvati became like cities.
As far as Samantapanchaka, the best of the twice-born, tiger among men, out of desire for tirthas, took to the river's bank.
As those sages of purified souls offered oblations there, the quarters were filled with great Vedic recitation.
With the agnihotras being offered by those great souls, the best of rivers shone, blazing on every side.
The Valakhilyas, O great king, the Ashmakuttas (stone-pounders), the ascetics who use their teeth as mortars, and others, the Samprakshalas,
ascetics living on air, on water, on leaves, bound by various restraints, sleeping on bare ground,
were the sages there near the Sarasvati, adorning the best of rivers as the gods adorn the Ganga.
Afterwards the sages who performed the sacrifice arrived, and the strict ones found no room in Kurukshetra.
Then by their sacred threads they marked out that tirtha, offered the agnihotras and performed various rites.
Then the Sarasvati, for their sake, O king of kings, showed herself to that company of sages, who were disappointed and anxious.
Then, making many groves, the best of rivers turned back, out of compassion for the sages of holy austerity, Janamejaya.
Having turned back for their sake, O king of kings, the Sarasvati, best of rivers, again flowed facing west.
My going is not in vain; I shall go to them again—so the great river worked that great wonder, O king.
Thus that grove, O king of kings, is called the Naimisheya grove at Kurukshetra, best of the Kurus; perform great rites.
Seeing there the many groves and the river turned back, the great-souled Rama was astonished.
Bathing there too, duly, the delight of the Yadus gave gifts to Brahmanas, vessels of various kinds, and various food and drink to the Brahmanas.
Then Bala proceeded, O king, honoured by the twice-born, to the best tirtha on the Sarasvati, thronged with hosts of Brahmanas,
adorned with jujube, ingudi, kashmarya, plaksha, ashvattha and vibhitaka trees, with jackfruit, palasha, karira and pilu,
with trees growing on the Sarasvati's bank, bandhana and syandana trees, with groves of parushaka, bilva and amrataka,
with clusters of atimukta and with parijata, abounding in plantain groves, beloved, lovely and charming,
and filled with many forest sages living on air, water, fruit and leaves, those who use their teeth as mortars, and the stone-pounders,
resounding with Vedic recitation, thronged with hundreds of herds of deer, constantly frequented by harmless men devoted to dharma.
The plough-bearer came to the Saptasarasvata tirtha, where the perfected great sage Mankanaka practised austerity.
Of what family was he born, and what had he studied, best of the twice-born? I wish to hear this duly, best of Brahmanas.
[Vaishampayana said:] "O king, there are seven Sarasvatis by which this world is pervaded; the Sarasvati is called by the mighty here and there.
Suprabha, Kanchanakshi, Vishala, Manasahrada Sarasvati, Oghavati, Suvenu and Vimalodaka.
When the great Grandsire's sacrifice was proceeding on the earth, in the vast sacrificial enclosure with the twice-born gathered,
with proclamations of auspicious days, spotless and the chanting of the Vedas, and the gods busy in that sacrificial rite,
there, great king, when the great-grandsire was consecrated, and the sacrifice was being performed with a session that fulfils all desires,
things thought of in the mind by those skilled in dharma and wealth came before the twice-born here and there, O king of kings.
Gandharvas sang there, hosts of Apsarases danced, and they played divine instruments with ease.
Even the gods were pleased at the splendour of that sacrifice and fell into supreme wonder, how much more beings of human birth.
While the sacrifice proceeded and the Grandsire was at Pushkara, the sages said, O king: "This sacrifice is not of great fruit, since the Sarasvati, best of rivers, is not seen here."
Hearing this, the revered one, pleased, remembered the Sarasvati; called by the sacrificing Grandsire at Pushkara, the Sarasvati there, O king of kings, was named Suprabha.
Seeing the swift Sarasvati, the sages were pleased; honouring the Grandsire, they thought highly of the sacrifice.
Thus this best of rivers, the Sarasvati at Pushkara, came into being for the Grandsire's sake and to please the wise.
The sages gathered at Naimisha, O king, and sat together; there were various discourses there about the Veda, lord of men.
There were sages there who knew various branches of Vedic study; gathering, those sages remembered the Sarasvati.
Being thought of by the sages performing the session, great king, the greatly fortunate holy Sarasvati came there to aid the assembled great souls.
At Naimisha, Kanchanakshi came for the sages performing the session; honoured there, Bharata, was the best of rivers.
For Gaya, who was sacrificing in the Gaya country, at the great rite, the best of rivers Sarasvati was invoked at Gaya's sacrifice.
The sages of keen vows call her Vishala at Gaya: that swift river born from the side of the Himalaya.
At the sacrifice of Auddalaki too, Bharata, as he sacrificed, when the circle of sages was assembled from all sides in great numbers,
in the holy northern part of Kosala, O king, the Sarasvati was thought of earlier by the sacrificing Auddalaki,
and the best of rivers came to that land for the sages, honoured by companies of sages clad in bark and deerskin; she is famed as Manohrada, for she was carried there by their minds.
Suvenu came at the holy Rishabhadvipa, frequented by royal sages, and the greatly fortunate Sarasvati, best of rivers, came to Kurukshetra for the great-souled Kuru as he sacrificed.
Oghavati too, O king of kings, was invoked at Kurukshetra by the great-souled Vasishtha, the Sarasvati of divine waters.
And for Daksha sacrificing at Gangadvara, the Sarasvati, the revered Vimalodaka, was again invoked by Brahma sacrificing, and went there to the holy Himalayan mountain.
United, they came together at that tirtha; hence it is known on earth as Saptasarasvata.
Thus the seven Sarasvatis have been named, and the Saptasarasvata tirtha is likewise remembered as holy.
Hear also of Mankanaka, the lifelong celibate, and the great sport he had, O king, when he plunged into the river.
Seeing a woman by chance in the water there, bathing in the Sarasvati, O great king, fair, with lovely sidelong glances, naked and blameless, his seed fell into the water.
The great ascetic took up that seed in a pitcher; divided sevenfold, it went in the pitcher, and from it seven sages were born, the hosts of the Maruts.
Vayuvega, Vayubala, Vayuha, Vayumandala, Vayujvala, Vayureta and the mighty Vayuchakra: these were born, the progenitors of the Maruts.
Hear this other, more wondrous thing on earth, O king of kings, the conduct of that great sage, as famed in the three worlds.
Of old, we have heard, the perfected Mankanaka was cut on the hand by a blade of kusha grass, O king, and vegetable juice flowed from it; seeing that sap, he was filled with joy and began to dance.
When he danced, all that is moving and unmoving danced, hero, both bewildered by his energy.
The gods led by Brahma and the sages rich in austerity, O king, petitioned Mahadeva for the sage's sake: "Do so, God, that he may not dance thus."
Then the god, seeing the sage greatly filled with joy, for the sake of the gods' welfare, Mahadeva spoke to him.
Ho, Brahmana who know dharma, why do you dance? What is the cause of this joy, best of sages, for an ascetic established in the path of dharma, best of the twice-born?
[The sage said:] "Do you not see, Brahmana, the vegetable sap that flows from my hand? Seeing it I dance with great joy, lord."
Laughing, the god said to the sage, bewildered by passion: "I am not astonished, Brahmana; behold me."
Having said this to the best of sages, the wise Mahadeva, O king of kings, struck his own thumb with the tip of his finger.
From the wound ash, like snow, came out, O king; seeing it, the sage was ashamed and fell at his feet.
[The sage said:] "I consider none other than Rudra a greater god than any; you, wielder of the trident, are the refuge of the world of gods and asuras.
The wise say that you created this universe; into you alone all enters again at the end of the age.
Even the gods cannot know you fully, how then I? In you, blameless one, all the gods led by Brahma are seen.
You are the maker and the cause of the gods; by your grace all the gods rejoice here, free of fear."
Thus praising Mahadeva, the sage said, bowing: "Revered one, by your grace may my austerity not waste away."
Then the god, pleased at heart, said again to the sage: "May your austerity increase a thousandfold by my grace, Brahmana; and I shall ever dwell with you in this hermitage.
Whoever worships me here at Saptasarasvata will find nothing hard to obtain here or hereafter; they will go to the world of the Sarasvati, without doubt."
This is the story of Mankanaka too, of great energy; he was born of the Wind to his own mother.
Having given gifts to the twice-born and fasted that night, honoured by the companies of sages, the plough-bearer rose in the morning,
took leave of all the sages and touched water, Bharata, and the mighty one swiftly set out, O king, for the sake of tirthas.
Then the plough-bearer came to the tirtha of Ushanas, called Kapalamochana, where the great sage was freed.
The great-bellied Mahodara, O great king, had his shin seized by a great head, the head of a Rakshasa cast by Rama of old.
There in former days Kavya (Shukra), great-souled, practised austerity; there all his policy appeared, and staying there he reflected on the strife between Daityas and Danavas.
Reaching that best of tirthas, O king, Bala gave wealth duly to the great-souled Brahmanas.
[Janamejaya said:] "How was Kapalamochana, Brahmana, where the great sage was freed? And how did the head cling to him, and for what reason?"
[Vaishampayana said:] "In former days, tiger among kings, when the great-souled Raghava lived in the Dandaka forest, Rakshasas were slain there.
At Janasthana the head of a wicked Rakshasa was cut off by a sharp-edged razor-arrow, and it fell in the great forest.
It clung to the shin of Mahodara, who was roaming in the forest by chance, O king, and pierced the bone and throbbed.
Because of that clinging, the twice-born, greatly wise, could not go to tirthas and sacred places.
Tormented by pain, with that foul discharge, the great sage, we have heard, went to all the tirthas on earth.
The great ascetic went to all rivers and seas and told all that to the sages of purified souls.
Bathing at all tirthas, he did not gain release; but that best of Brahmanas heard the great word of the sages
about the best tirtha of the Sarasvati, then famed as that of Ushanas, destroyer of all sin, an unsurpassed perfected field.
Going there, the Brahmana came to the tirtha of Ushanas; and as he touched the water at the tirtha of Ushanas, the head, releasing his leg, fell into the water.
Then, free of pain, O king, with purified soul, free of stain, Mahodara came to his hermitage, pleased, his task done.
Having gone to his holy hermitage, freed, the great ascetic told all that to the sages of purified souls.
Hearing his words, honourer of others, the assembled sages named that tirtha Kapalamochana.
Having given many gifts there and honoured the Brahmanas, Madhava, best of the Vrishnis, then went to the hermitage of Rushangu.
There Arshtishena practised dreadful austerity, Bharata, and there the great sage Vishvamitra obtained Brahmanhood.
Then the glorious plough-bearer, surrounded by Brahmanas, went, O king of kings, where Rushangu gave up his body.
Rushangu, an aged Brahmana, always devoted to austerity, Bharata, resolved to lay down his body after much deliberation.
Then, taking all his sons, the great ascetic Rushangu said there, "Take me to Prithudaka."
Knowing Rushangu to be advanced in age, those ascetics brought the ascetic to that tirtha of the Sarasvati.
By those sons the wise one was brought to the holy Sarasvati, with hundreds of tirthas, frequented by companies of Brahmanas.
There, O king, the great ascetic, bathed duly, and knowing the merits of the tirtha, the best of sages, greatly pleased, tiger among men, said this to all his sons who attended him:
On the northern bank of the Sarasvati, whoever gives up his body at Prithudaka while reciting prayers, death will not torment him afterwards.
Bathing there, the righteous-souled plough-bearer touched the water and gave many gifts to the Brahmanas, he who was fond of Brahmanas.
There the revered Grandsire of the worlds created the worlds, where Arshtishena, O Kaurava, of keen vows, the best of sages, obtained Brahmanhood by great austerity.
Where the royal sage Sindhudvipa, the great ascetic Devapi, and the great sage Vishvamitra, the revered one of fierce splendour and great austerity, obtained Brahmanhood,
there came the strong, glorious Balabhadra.
And how did Devapi, Brahmana, and Vishvamitra, best of men—tell me that, revered one; my curiosity is great.
[Vaishampayana said:] "Of old, in the Krita age, O king, the best of the twice-born Arshtishena, dwelling in his teacher's house, was ever engaged in study.
Though he lived always in his teacher's house, O king, his learning was not completed, nor the Vedas, lord of men.
Disheartened, O king, the great ascetic practised austerity; then by that austerity he obtained the unsurpassed Vedas.
Learned, versed in the Veda and perfected, the best of sages, the great ascetic, gave three boons at that tirtha.
'At this tirtha of the great river, from today a man who bathes shall obtain the abundant fruit of a horse sacrifice.
From today there shall be no fear here of beasts of prey, and with little effort one shall gain abundant fruit.'
Having said this, the greatly radiant sage went to heaven. Thus the revered, glorious Arshtishena became perfected.
And likewise Kaushika, dear one, ever devoted to austerity, with senses subdued, obtained Brahmanhood by well-practised austerity.
There was a great kshatriya named Gadhi, famed on earth; his son was the glorious Vishvamitra, O king.
The king Kaushika, dear one, became, it is said, a great yogin; having anointed his son Vishvamitra, the great ascetic
set his mind on laying down his body; the people, bowing, said to him, "Do not go, greatly wise one; save us from great fear."
Thus addressed, Gadhi replied to the people: "My son will be the protector of the whole world."
Having said this, Gadhi installed Vishvamitra and went to heaven, O king; Vishvamitra became king, but though he tried he could not protect the earth.
Then the king heard of great fear from the Rakshasas and set out from the city with a fourfold army.
Having gone a long way, he came to Vasishtha's hermitage, and his soldiers there, O king, did many wrongs.
Then the revered Brahmana Vasishtha came to the hermitage and saw the great forest being broken all round.
Angry, great king, the best of sages Vasishtha said to his cow, "Create dreadful Shabaras."
So told, the cow created men of dreadful aspect, and they, reaching that army, broke it in every direction.
Seeing the army routed, Vishvamitra, son of Gadhi, thinking austerity supreme, set his mind on austerity alone.
At this best of tirthas of the Sarasvati, O king, composed, wasting his body by restraints and fasts,
he lived on water, on air, and on leaves, slept on bare ground, and kept other separate restraints.
The gods repeatedly obstructed his vows, but the great soul's mind did not swerve from his restraint.
Then, practising many kinds of austerity with great effort, the son of Gadhi became like the sun in splendour.
The Grandsire, of great splendour, thought Vishvamitra thus endowed with austerity worthy of a boon, and offered him one.
He chose a boon, O king: "May I be a Brahmana." "So be it," said Brahma, Grandsire of all the worlds.
Having obtained Brahmanhood by fierce austerity, the greatly renowned one roamed the whole earth, his desires fulfilled, like a god.
At that best of tirthas Rama gave various wealth, milch cows, vehicles and beds,
clothes, ornaments, fine food and drink, glad, honouring the best of the twice-born, O king.
Then, O king, Rama went to the nearby hermitage of Baka, where, it is heard, Dalbhya Baka practised intense austerity.
Then, making a soft sound, as though a bird hiding itself, he sought a branch of the banyan tree, Bharata.
[Vidura said:] "Rise, O king; why do you lie there? Steady yourself by yourself; this is the settled lot of all mortals, moving and unmoving.
By that my heart burns greatly, a slayer of my brother; with Karna and Arjuna as allies I could even conquer Vasava (Indra).
[Death said:] "If there were no cause, you would not be the doer either; you are the cause of the destruction, therefore in my view you are to be punished."
You are surely faithless, dull-witted, your memory lost; do not be so; such ignorance is not fit for you.
And Gandhari, daughter of Subala, casting off her grief for her sons, was always affectionate to him, as to her own sons.
At sunrise and sunset in that city the sun was repeatedly seen surrounded by headless trunks of men.
I formerly obtained this from Varuna for a reason, Partha; the Gandiva, best of bows, should be given back to Varuna.
[Vaishampayana said:] Having said this to him, the gods then assigned a divine messenger: "Show Yudhishthira his friends, scorcher of foes."
